item.text: [{"taxonId":56917,"summary":"A genus of prostrate perennial aquatic or semi-aquatic plants occurring across tropical and temperate regions worldwide. Its creeping stems often root at the nodes and form dense mats around water, carrying round or kidney-shaped leaves with scalloped edges.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2","s1:p3"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":56955,"summary":"A genus of annual and perennial flowering plants native to the Americas, chiefly North America. Its broad heads comprise many tiny flowers, while young heads track the sun by day and return east overnight; mature flowering heads generally remain east-facing.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Documented foods come from particular species: H. annuus seeds and oil, and H. tuberosus tubers.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p6","s1:p14","s1:p15","s2:p2"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p23"]}},{"taxonId":57022,"summary":"A cosmopolitan genus of mostly aquatic or moisture-loving sedges. Its green stems perform photosynthesis while its leaves are reduced to basal sheaths, and every species bears flowers in a single unbranched spikelet at each stem tip.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Within the genus, Chinese water chestnut has rhizome tubers eaten peeled, raw or boiled.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p4"]}},{"taxonId":57066,"summary":"An annual or biennial legume native to Eurasia and introduced to North America, Africa and Australia. It has three-part leaves, yellow spring-to-summer flowers and a characteristic sweet odor; its seeds can remain viable for up to 30 years.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":57067,"summary":"A genus of annual, biennial or perennial legumes native to Europe, Asia and Africa. Melilots bear narrow three-part leaves and loose clusters of mostly white or yellow flowers; their sweet-smelling tissues contain coumarin, which molds can convert into toxic dicoumarol in decaying plants.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p4","s1:p9"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":57115,"summary":"A mint-family genus occurring in Central and South America, Mexico, California, Hispaniola and Hawaii; the Hawaiian species is probably a human introduction. Many species bear attractive pitcher-shaped flowers, often in shades of purple.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":57156,"summary":"An annual cereal grass descended from wild Avena sterilis whose ancestral forms grew in the Fertile Crescent. Common oat thrives in cool, wet summers and produces edible grain commonly rolled or crushed into oatmeal or ground into flour.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"The grain is eaten as oatmeal, porridge, flour, baked goods, breakfast cereals and oat-milk products.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p9","s1:p18","s1:p51"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p3","s1:p51"]}},{"taxonId":57159,"summary":"A grass genus widespread across much of Africa, Eurasia and Latin America. Its flimsy upright stems form tussocks, with flat or curved leaves and compact summer flower clusters composed of short-stalked spikelets.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":57168,"summary":"A large grass genus occurring across all inhabited continents and many islands. Lovegrasses commonly serve as livestock fodder; their seeds are tiny and cumbersome to gather, although teff is a commercially important crop used for traditional breads in the Horn of Africa.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Documented edible members include teff for breads; E. clelandii and E. tremula are recorded as famine foods.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p4"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p4"]}},{"taxonId":57182,"summary":"A cereal grass whose wild form ranges from North Africa and Crete to Tibet, common barley was first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent. Its spikelets form a herringbone-patterned, bristly ear, and its edible grain is used in soups, breads, malt, beer and whisky.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"After the inedible outer hull is removed, grain is eaten in breads, soups, stews and porridge, or malted for beer and whisky.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3","s1:p8","s1:p15"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p3","s1:p45","s1:p46","s1:p58"]}}]
